learningObjective: Explain why deep-learning runtimes use a caching memory allocator (a pool of previously freed device blocks) instead of calling cudaMalloc/cudaFree per tensor.
stem: Deep-learning runtimes (PyTorch, TensorFlow, TVM) implement a caching memory allocator on the GPU rather than calling `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` for each tensor. Which reason is the strongest?

options.text: `cudaMalloc` and `cudaFree` are synchronous with respect to all CUDA streams and take microseconds to milliseconds; calling them on every tensor allocation would serialize the stream and dominate end-to-end latency. A caching allocator amortizes this by pooling freed blocks and reusing them without touching the driver.

`cudaMalloc` returns memory that cannot be used as a kernel argument until a `cudaMemcpy` initializes it; a caching allocator writes zeros lazily so kernels can read uninitialized memory safely without additional API calls.

The CUDA driver limits the number of live allocations per process to 1024; a caching allocator sidesteps this by keeping a single large allocation for the lifetime of the process regardless of workload.

A caching allocator eliminates memory fragmentation entirely because it always returns exactly the requested size and rounds up to a multiple of one byte, meaning no wasted padding ever occurs across tensor lifetimes.

explanation: `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` synchronize with the device and cost microseconds to milliseconds — orders of magnitude more than a well-tuned pool lookup. A caching allocator holds freed device blocks in size-classed pools and reuses them on subsequent allocation requests, avoiding the driver call in the fast path. Fragmentation is a real concern; the allocator manages it via block splitting/coalescing but does not eliminate it (D is false). B and C fabricate driver behavior.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: this is the documented motivation for PyTorch's caching allocator and equivalent designs.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: cudaMalloc'd memory is usable as a kernel argument; nothing forces zero-init.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: there is no such 1024-allocation limit.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: caching allocators still have fragmentation; they mitigate it but do not eliminate it.

assumptions: The workload allocates and frees tensors frequently (training steps, iterative decoding), so per-step allocator cost matters.
nonImplications: Does not imply that caching allocators are always ideal; long-running services may need periodic empty-cache calls to release memory back to the OS.
Does not imply fragmentation is negligible; long training runs with variable shapes can suffer OOM from fragmentation.

performanceClaim.scope: Frequent-allocation ML workloads on NVIDIA GPUs
